Note that while the latest commit ([6738eb5](https://github.com/apify/impit/pull/28/commits/6738eb5e54d1d0649b7b7536f399c72d69367fe3)) simplifies our codebase a lot, there is a few drawbacks:
- We'd have to drop the support for Node <18 (due to the use of `Response` from `fetch` API). The broken tests on that commit suggest that there are some unimplemented interfaces even in Node 18.
- We'd have to drop our [glorious `.text()` implementation](https://github.com/apify/impit/blob/master/impit/src/response_parsing/mod.rs) with byte stream prescan, BOM sniffing, and more. Since consuming the JS `ReadableStream` is an async task (either in JS or Rust), and since we cannot safely use the `Env` reference inside of an async function, it's a serious hairball.

Food for thought - maybe we want to drop the entire `ImpitResponse` class and return a `new Response()` JS instance altogether? I.e. push the headers, status code etc. in there as well? I don't really see any problem with this, but maybe it might tie our hands later (e.g. see the custom `text()` implementation problem above).

OK, I won't notify you again about this release, but will get in touch when a new version is available. If you'd rather skip all updates until the next major or minor version, let me know by commenting `@dependabot ignore this major version` or `@dependabot ignore this minor version`.

If you change your mind, just re-open this PR and I'll resolve any conflicts on it.

> Flakiness seems to be much lower than when we used the "official" instance. It's not 100%, but close enough in my opinion.

You summed it up perfectly 🙂.

Upon deeper inspection, this seems more like a Client Hints via ALPS (Application layer protocol settings) issue.

See that the Unexpected Message (`0x02 0x0a`) TLS Alert comes right after the Client sends the `HTTP/2` headers. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8c132f72-2d3f-4001-8cab-723cfe31a132)

In the ALPN/ALPS extension message, the server picks HTTP/2 and sends an ALPS message containing what seems like HTTP header names:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a74e37cb-141b-4e7e-a11a-30adc89dad0a)

Unfortunately, making `impit` send those headers doesn't solve this issue.

Removing the `ALPS` extension from the `ClientHello` sent by Impit does make the requests work. 
For now, we could mitigate this issue like this, but this makes Impit more detectable (as it directly modifies - among others - its JA4 fingerprint).
huh, did this really broke usage in ESM projects? and how come things work fine when we were testing it in crawlee? those projects were also ESM

Right - the other way around - this might have broken usage in CJS projects. 

I'm assuming this broke the Crawlee E2E tests on Platform, as we run Local and Memory by importing directly from the `test.mjs` scripts (ESM context), but on Platform, we first build it with `tsc` (with `tsconfig.json` extending `@apify/tsconfig`, so it compiles with `module: CommonJS`).

see the bad run e.g. here:

https://console.apify.com/view/runs/bic7Rmg3L4sh4yF8n

But impit is CJS, there is no native ESM build, the same code was executed regardless of the caller being CJS or ESM.

I am just confused that this ever worked, regardless of the project using it was CJS/ESM.

Ah, took me a while, but I think I got to the bottom of this. My guess would still be on some transpilation tool adding a shim for `exports` (better than Node does). Those tools (like ESBuild) are abundant in our projects because of the usage of TypeScript and frameworks like `vite`, which just make everything work automagically.

See this JS example mixing ESM and CJS syntax - `node ./esm.js` will fail with the `"Identifier 'exports' has already been declared"`.

![obrazek](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/88f07df3-c645-4c28-9f95-b442e9e39c47)

Now see e.g. this [example from esbuild](https://esbuild.github.io/try/#YgAwLjI1LjAALS1mb3JtYXQ9ZXNtIC0tb3V0ZGlyPXRlc3QAZQBjanMuanMAY29uc3QgZXhwb3J0cyA9ICJub3Qtd2hhdC15b3UnZC1leHBlY3QiCgptb2R1bGUuZXhwb3J0cy5tZXNzYWdlID0gZXhwb3J0czsAZQBlc20uanMAaW1wb3J0IHsgbWVzc2FnZSB9IGZyb20gJy4vY2pzLmpzJw) with `--format=esm` - when transpiled, ESBuild will rename the original `exports` shim to `exports2` to avoid conflict (so the result will be executable).

![obrazek](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/145f3ac9-630d-4d1c-b93e-222e4906d923)

You're still right that it's weird that this would touch the code from dependencies. 🤔 

Also, I'm not sure what the takeaway from this is. Maybe that we should add e2e tests to `impit`? :)

is this really enough? i dont think so, we had to generate a separate `index.mjs` to make this work in other projects, thats what the `gen-esm-wrapper` is doing for us (here its fine to do it by hand). and then you also need to mention that file in package.json exports field.

As far as named exports (`import { name } from 'cjs-module'`) support goes, I'm fairly positive this should be enough.

See [Node.JS docs on this topic](https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html#commonjs-namespaces) - CJS files are statically analysed for named imports using [this grammar](https://github.com/nodejs/cjs-module-lexer/tree/2.0.0?tab=readme-ov-file#grammar), which generates the syntax from this PR, but didn't generate - in the formal languages lingo - the previous one (opaque assign to `module.exports`).

It's not really a critic problem 🙂. Rather, it's a point that can cause a bit of confusion for Python users.

`Httpx` was originally inspired by the `requests` API. Requests only had a `data` parameter.

As the library evolved, they modified their API by separating `content` for raw data and `data` for forms. Although the typing indicates otherwise, at this point `data` completely replaces `content` in `httpx`. They plan to [finally drop this behavior only in version 1.0](https://www.python-httpx.org/compatibility/#request-content:~:text=Using%20the%20data%3D%3Ctext/byte%20content%3E%20will%20raise%20a%20deprecation%20warning%2C%20and%20is%20expected%20to%20be%20fully%20removed%20with%20the%20HTTPX%201.0%20release.). 

From my point of view the `data` parameter can be confusing for those who know it from the `requests` days and use libraries inspired by their API. Perhaps we could use a similar but more transparent name, `form_data`?

I see that `@crawlee/impit-client` has `"impit": "^0.2.1"` (see the `^` caret symbol) in the dependencies, so your package manager should install the latest (`0.3.0`) version automatically on `npm install`. Maybe you'll need to remove `package-lock.json` and / or `node_modules` to enforce installation of the latest versions of the packages. Let us know if if helps!

I would prefer to completely match the API of `httpx` for easier adoption of `impit` by random Python devs. IMO our endgame is to allow people to do:

```diff
-from httpx import Client

```

This is intended behaviour, as reusing the same `Impit` instance allows for HTTP connection pooling (reusing the underlying TLS / TCP resources for multiple subsequent requests).

HTTP connection pooling (and other resource-sharing notions, e.g. HTTP/2 internals) are not possible when using different proxies for different requests (two requests going to the same endpoint cannot use the same TCP connection if they are told to go through different proxies). 

We'd prefer to communicate this idea in our interface too - the fact that you have to create a new `Impit` instance when switching proxies shows what's actually happening under the hood (Impit has to open a new socket, go through the TLS handshake etc.)

> What would need to be supported there to make it viable for impit?

Mostly the monorepo-related options, like `--include-path` and `--ignore-tags`. Currently (if I'm not mistaken), `git-cliff-release` doesn't allow the use of commits only concerning a given folder/set of files. 

Using an "everything" changelog in this project would require us to publish possibly unchanged packages (e.g., on `pip`, just because we made changes in the `npm` package).

If this proves useful here, I'll be happy to move some | all of the tweaks I used here to `git-cliff-release`.

### Example usage

```python
from http.cookiejar import CookieJar

cookie_jar = CookieJar()

impit = Client(
    browser=browser,
    cookie_jar=cookie_jar,
)

impit.post("https://example.com/login") # sets cookie
impit.get("https://example.com/admin") # impit sends the cookie, authenticating itself with the server

assert len(cookie_jar) == 1 # user can process the cookies, persisting them, using them with other impit instances etc.
```


Unfortunately, the `Cookie` class constructor has 16 required kwargs, making the usage quite unergonomic. Ideas for a better API are welcome.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d30387be-29d3-4a49-be85-c060bbca5742)

Additionally, we are moving away from the `httpx` interface here. `httpx` has `cookies` constructor parameter (not `cookie_jar`), which accepts their [helper class instance](https://www.python-httpx.org/api/#cookies) (just wrapping `http.cookiejar.CookieJar` with convenience methods).

>  Ideas for a better API are welcome.

Perhaps we could add our own class wrapper around `CookieJar`. Like `httpx` does (and probably all Python clients do, since the `CookieJar` API is not userfrendly). Something simple at this stage, maybe just two methods `set_cookie` and `get_cookies` and `jar` property. Then we can base use case reduce to only 2 parameters `name`, `value` as in `httpx`.

In `crawlee-python` we also use a wrapper class - https://github.com/apify/crawlee-python/blob/master/src/crawlee/sessions/_cookies.py#L58

- maybe support for passing interface names (e.g. `lo`, `eth1` etc?) There is `reqwest.ClientBuilder` [`interface` option](https://docs.rs/reqwest/latest/reqwest/struct.ClientBuilder.html#method.interface), but that is not available on Windows.

### Deeper Analysis: The Missing User Activation Context

The core realization is that the presence of `Sec-Fetch-User` is **not** solely determined by `Sec-Fetch-Dest`. It depends critically on whether the request was triggered by a direct **user activation** (like a click).

My initial issue correctly identified that for destinations like `image` or `script`, `Sec-Fetch-User` should be omitted. However, I incorrectly assumed that for `Sec-Fetch-Dest: document`, the `Sec-Fetch-User: ?1` header should always be present. This is not true.

Here are critical scenarios where `Sec-Fetch-Dest` is a navigation target, but a real browser correctly **omits** the `Sec-Fetch-User` header:

1.  **HTTP Redirects:** When a user clicks a link, the first request has `Sec-Fetch-User: ?1`. If the server responds with a 3xx redirect, the browser's automatic follow-up request still has `Sec-Fetch-Dest: document`, but it will **not** have the `Sec-Fetch-User` header, as it was initiated by the server, not the user.

2.  **JavaScript-Initiated Navigation:** A navigation triggered by `window.location.href` inside a `setTimeout` will have `Sec-Fetch-Dest: document` but no `Sec-Fetch-User` header, because the user activation has expired.

This reveals that `impit` cannot infer the correct behavior from the provided headers alone. To address this, I'd like to propose potential solution.

---
### Proposal: A "Magic Value" to Omit Header

As an alternative that avoids changing the API, `impit` could treat a specific value for `Sec-Fetch-User` as a special signal to omit the header entirely. The value `'?0'` is a good candidate.

**New Logic:**
1. If the user provides `Sec-Fetch-User: '?0'`, the library removes the header from the final request.
2. If the user provides no `Sec-Fetch-User` header, the library uses its default logic.
3. If the user provides any other value (e.g., `'?1'`), it is sent as is.

**Example Usage:**
```javascript
// Simulate a redirect by using the "magic value" to omit the header
await impit.fetch(redirectedUrl, {
    headers: { 
        "Sec-Fetch-Dest": "document",
        "Sec-Fetch-User": "?0" 
    }
});
// Result: The Sec-Fetch-User header is correctly OMITTED.
```

**Trade-offs:**
*   **Pro:** No breaking API changes. Provides the necessary control.
*   **Con:** Less discoverable than an explicit flag. The default behavior remains suboptimal.

Hi @IamsadVN, thank you for your interest in this project!

Until `0.5.4`, impit (via its upstream dependencies) did not actually support SOCKS4 proxies correctly. When you passed a `socks4://` proxy, the traffic was not routed through the proxy at all - it was connecting directly to the target server. I confirmed this with Wireshark captures and also with the new tests we just added: [#268](https://github.com/apify/impit/pull/268).

This means that in your script, what seemed like working SOCKS4 proxy support in `0.5.3` was in fact just a direct connection. In `0.5.4`, the behavior was fixed, so SOCKS4 proxies are now handled properly. If the proxy you’re trying doesn’t support SOCKS4 correctly (or has connectivity issues), you’ll now see connection errors instead of a silent fallback.

If you’d like to double-check your proxy, you can test it with a standalone tool like:

```bash
curl --socks4 <ip:port> https://targetserver.com
```

(or `--socks5` for SOCKS5). That way, you’ll know for sure whether the proxy and the target server are alive and responding.

Since this is the intended behavior after the fix, I’ll go ahead and close this issue. Thank you for bringing this up.

In my project, I need to query a large number of pixel coordinates from an external API. For each pixel, I must use a different proxy, so my script creates a new `Impit` instance for every request. The usage pattern looks like this:

1. **For each pixel request**, I create a new `Impit` instance with the following options:

   * `proxyUrl` (rotated on every request),
   * `timeout: 6000`,
   * `browser: "firefox"`,
   * `ignoreTlsErrors: true`,
   * `http3: true`.
     This means my script may instantiate `Impit` thousands of times during a full scan.

2. After creating the instance, I call `impit.fetch("https://place34.com/api/pixel/...")`.
   If `fetch` throws an error (which happens often with unstable proxies), I retry the same request inside a loop until it completes without an exception. The logic is essentially:
   “try `fetch`, and if it fails, repeat again using the same instance.”

3. In the main execution flow, I build a list of pixel requests and execute them in **batches of 50**.
   This results in multiple `Impit` instances running concurrently — typically around 50 at a time.
   Each batch is awaited with `Promise.all`.

4. When a request finally succeeds, I check `response.ok`, parse the JSON if available, and write the result to a text file.
   If it is not painted, I log that information instead.

So in summary, my usage pattern is:

* **One new `Impit` instance per request** (because each request needs a different proxy).
* **Multiple instances running in parallel** (50 per batch).
* **Each instance may retry `fetch` several times** until it resolves without throwing.
* The process repeats for a large number of pixel coordinates, resulting in many instantiations of `Impit`.

Apologies for the delay in getting back to this.

After further consideration, we've decided to close this issue as not planned. Impit is deterministic - for a given browser profile, the generated headers are always the same, so there's no hidden randomness that would require runtime inspection. This is no different from any other HTTP client or user-agent implementation, which also doesn't expose its internal header merging process.

Regarding request signing specifically — per [RFC 9421](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421#name-the-signature-input-http-fi), the signer chooses which components to include in the signature. Other implementations (e.g. AWS Signature V4), might require you to serialize the entire request, but as per the first paragraph, Impit doesn't introduce random or unpredictable headers that would make this any different from other HTTP clients

As for conditioning application logic on the generated fingerprint - we'd consider that a design concern better addressed at the application level rather than something the library should facilitate.

That said, we will prepare better documentation on how to override HTTP headers and the priority rules that apply when user-provided headers interact with fingerprint-generated ones. This should help with the debugging and verification use cases you mentioned.

Thank you for the detailed write-up and for using Impit!
Closing due to inactivity.

How do we know which exact headers are being sent?

Re-measured this on `0.13.0` today, five months on. Two of the five discrepancies have since been fixed; three remain, and I think I can narrow down the `WINDOW_UPDATE` one.

**Current state vs. the original report:**

| SETTING | reported (Feb) | impit today | real Chrome 150 | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `HEADER_TABLE_SIZE` (1) | not sent | not sent | `65536` | ❌ |
| `ENABLE_PUSH` (2) | `0` | `0` | `0` | ✅ |
| `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (4) | `2097152` | `6291456` | `6291456` | ✅ fixed |
| `MAX_FRAME_SIZE` (5) | `16384` sent | `16384` sent | not sent | ❌ |
| `MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE` (6) | `16384` | `262144` | `262144` | ✅ fixed |
| `WINDOW_UPDATE` | `5177345` | `15597570` | `15663105` | ❌ close |

```
impit chrome142 : 2:0;4:6291456;5:16384;6:262144|15597570|0|m,a,s,p
real Chrome 150 : 1:65536;2:0;4:6291456;6:262144|15663105|0|m,a,s,p
```

My real-Chrome measurement matches the "Real Chrome" line in your original report exactly, so that reference still holds on Chrome 150.

The core finding is unchanged: `chrome131`, `chrome136` and `chrome142` all produce the **byte-identical** HTTP/2 fingerprint, so profile selection still changes TLS but not HTTP/2.

## The `WINDOW_UPDATE` gap looks like a double subtraction

The remaining difference is exactly `65535`, and the arithmetic lines up cleanly:

```
15 MiB                 = 15728640
15728640 - 65535       = 15663105   <- real Chrome
15728640 - 2 × 65535   = 15597570   <- impit
```

Both are 15 MiB minus the default 65535 initial connection window — impit just subtracts it twice. That would be consistent with passing an already-net value into `http2_initial_connection_window_size()` when the underlying layer also subtracts the default before emitting the `WINDOW_UPDATE` increment. Passing the gross `15728640` (rather than a pre-subtracted `15663105`) may be all that's needed there.

That leaves `HEADER_TABLE_SIZE` — still the one that needs the upstream reqwest/h2 change you mentioned — and the spurious `MAX_FRAME_SIZE`, which Chrome omits entirely.

## Reproduction

```js
import { Impit } from "impit";

for (const browser of ["chrome131", "chrome136", "chrome142"]) {
  const res = await new Impit({ browser }).fetch("https://tls.peet.ws/api/all");
  console.log(browser, (await res.json()).http2.akamai_fingerprint);
}
```

Environment: impit `0.13.0`, Node 22, Windows x64. Reference: Google Chrome 150 via Playwright `channel: "chrome"`.

| layer | `header_table_size` | omit `max_frame_size` |
| --- | --- | --- |

default. Omission is representable below reqwest, but:

```rust
// reqwest-0.13.2, src/async_impl/client.rs:950
if let Some(http2_max_frame_size) = config.http2_max_frame_size {

}
```

reference: every setting takes `impl Into<Option<u32>>`, so unset means omitted rather than
